news.title: Rubio greets India on Independence Day, says US ties stronger than ever
news.text: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Friday greeted the people of India on the country’s 80th Independence Day and said the bilateral relationship was stronger than ever. He said the ties had continued to grow because of the personal relationship between President Donald Trump and Prime Minister Narendra Modi.Rubio said the friendship and family links between the people of the two countries formed the base of a partnership that was innovative, resilient and forward-looking. He also highlighted cooperation across key sectors, while several states in the US and a number of American lawmakers marked the occasion with greetings and proclamations.In a statement, Rubio said, "On behalf of the United States of America, I extend warm congratulations to the people of India on their Independence Day." He added, "Thanks to the personal relationship between President Trump and Prime Minister Modi, the US-India relationship continues to grow and is stronger than ever."Rubio said US-India collaboration was making both countries, and the wider Indian Ocean region, safer, stronger and more prosperous. He referred to cooperation in defence, energy security, critical minerals, artificial intelligence, space cooperation and commerce. "The deep ties of friendship and family between our two peoples form the foundation of a partnership that is innovative, resilient, and forward-looking. The United States looks forward to the future our two countries will build together," he said.Several states across the US have issued special proclamations to commemorate August 15, 2026, as ‘India Day’ to mark India’s independence, underlining the growing contribution of the Indian diaspora to American life. A number of senators, Congress members, lawmakers and city councils have also extended greetings on India’s Independence Day, rounding off a message from the US that focused on strong bilateral ties and growing people-to-people links.With PTI Inputs- EndsPublished By: India Today Web Desk Published On: Aug 15, 2026 06:22 IST

news.title: BBC Donald Trump Defamation Lawsuit: Ivanka Trunp, Donald Trump Jr, Jared Kushner Dragged Into $10 Billion Battle
news.text: The BBC is seeking to question three members of Donald Trump's family as part of its defence against the US President's $10bn defamation lawsuit, according to court documents. The broadcaster wants subpoenas issued to Donald Trump Jr, Ivanka Trump and Jared Kushner, arguing they may have first-hand information about Trump's intentions when he delivered his 6 January 2021 speech. The subpoenas seek both testimony under oath and documents. The BBC says Donald Trump Jr and Ivanka Trump were present when their father revised parts of the speech and were also at the Ellipse while he addressed supporters as the attack on the US Capitol was unfolding. It also says Kushner prepared a proposed statement for Trump condemning the violence. The broadcaster argues that evidence about what Trump intended to communicate is relevant to whether a 2024 BBC Panorama documentary gave a materially false impression and whether the BBC acted with the level of intent required for a defamation claim involving a public figure. The legal dispute centres on the documentary, which edited together separate sections of Trump's January 6 speech. The editing made statements delivered at different points appear to form a continuous passage, creating the impression that Trump had directly called for violent action. The BBC later apologised for the editing and acknowledged that it had created a misleading impression. It has nevertheless denied that the documentary provides grounds for Trump's defamation claims. Trump filed the lawsuit in December 2025. He is seeking $5bn in damages for alleged defamation and a further $5bn under Florida legislation covering deceptive and unfair trade practices. The case is being heard in federal court in Florida. Court filings show that the BBC has encountered difficulties serving the proposed subpoenas. An attempt to serve Trump and Kushner at their Miami home was blocked by police. A US Secret Service lawyer subsequently told the BBC that the agency was not authorised to accept subpoenas on their behalf. A separate attempt to serve Trump Jr at the Trump Organization's offices in Trump Tower in New York was also unsuccessful. The BBC has asked the court to allow alternative methods of service, including sending the subpoenas by mail or through lawyers representing the President. A subpoena generally needs to be properly served before a court can compel a person to comply. A federal magistrate judge has previously allowed the BBC to pursue discovery involving members of Trump's inner circle. Last month, US Magistrate Judge Enjoliqué Lett ruled that the subpoenas were sufficiently connected to the allegations in Trump's lawsuit, while indicating that some requests could later be narrowed. The BBC has reportedly issued dozens of subpoenas seeking information from members of Trump's family and former administration, as well as other people and government bodies. The family subpoenas are part of a wider battle over evidence in the case. Trump's lawsuit initially alleged that the BBC documentary had caused extensive economic and reputational damage, including harm to his businesses, properties and personal brand. The BBC therefore sought financial records from the Donald J Trump Revocable Trust. Judge Lett ruled in July that Trump had put his financial interests at issue by claiming economic losses and ordered the production of a narrower set of financial records. Trump subsequently sought permission to amend his complaint and potentially remove claims relating to economic damages. US District Judge Roy Altman temporarily paused the financial discovery while considering that request.
news.summary: The broadcaster claims they possess vital information regarding Trump's intentions during his January 6 speech, which is central to the lawsuit involving a Panorama documentary that allegedly misrepresented his statements

news.title: Trump wanted to cripple Iran - now he might be handing Tehran a victory - opinion
news.text: You almost have to pinch yourself watching what is unfolding between the United States and Iran.US President Donald Trump entered this confrontation promising American dominance: that Iran would never obtain a nuclear weapon, its missile-production capability would be destroyed, and its support for terrorist proxies would be severed. America would no longer be threatened, extorted, or played.After the first American attack, Trump had something concrete to show for those words: the US directly struck Iran's nuclear facilities.After America's second bombing campaign, the question is far more uncomfortable: What exactly did America win?Israel reportedly wanted to participate in the latest American strikes, but Washington did not want Israel involved. This became America's operation, America's targets, and America's strategy.That distinction matters.Trump wanted America to take the lead. America took ownership.Now America owns the outcome.Iran's regime survived. Its nuclear ambitions remain unresolved. Its missile and drone capabilities are being rebuilt. Russia and China remain sources of weapons, components, and assistance.And now Iran has turned the Strait of Hormuz into leverage against the US. Washington is reportedly considering gradually releasing frozen Iranian funds and providing partial sanctions relief in return for Iran allowing unrestricted, toll-free commercial passage through Hormuz.How did America get from Trump's demands for Iranian surrender to negotiating what Tehran receives for reopening an international waterway?Trump says America has “total control” of Hormuz. If America has total control, why is Iran setting the price?That is what makes this so embarrassing for America – and particularly for a president whose global brand is strength.The danger goes much further than appearances.Trump's own administration has argued that denying Iran revenue is essential because Tehran uses its resources for missiles, drones, the Revolutionary Guards, and terrorist proxies.Loosening sanctions therefore doesn't exist in a vacuum.Money is fungible. Economic breathing room can free Iranian resources for rebuilding missiles, strengthening Hezbollah, supporting the Houthis and Hamas, restoring military infrastructure, and potentially advancing the nuclear capabilities America just went to war to stop.America cannot spend billions destroying Iran's military machine and then help create the financial conditions for Iran to rebuild it.All because Iran disrupted Hormuz? That would send a catastrophic message far beyond Tehran.And Hamas will be watching.Trump created the Board of Peace and the International Stabilization Force for Gaza as part of his plan to end the Gaza conflict. The ISF is supposed to support Hamas's disarmament, prevent terrorist infrastructure from being rebuilt, and help establish a new Palestinian police force.What happens to the credibility of that structure if Hamas watches its patron Iran challenge America, disrupt international commerce, survive American bombing, and then potentially obtain financial concessions?The lesson becomes dangerous:Hold out long enough, create enough pressure, violate agreements, make the political cost painful enough, and eventually Washington may renegotiate.That puts Israel's immediate borders at risk – not merely from Iranian missiles hundreds of miles away, but from Hamas and other armed groups directly next door.There is another regional development that deserves attention.The Middle East around Israel is reorganizingEgypt, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, and Turkey all sit within Trump's Board of Peace framework. Separately, Saudi Arabia has moved into a new defense arrangement with Turkey and Pakistan and is building broader regional security coalitions.None of that automatically makes those countries enemies of Israel. Saudi Arabia has never been formally at war with Israel in the modern era, and Egypt has maintained its peace treaty with Israel for decades.But something important has changed.Countries Washington hoped would become pillars of a new regional order alongside Israel are increasingly coordinating among themselves, building independent security structures and pursuing interests that do not necessarily align with Jerusalem's.That was always the risk.When these new structures were celebrated, the question should never have been simply whether Arab and Muslim countries were finally uniting.The question was: Uniting around what – and ultimately, against whom?What was presented as a framework that could surround Israel with stability can become something very different if Israel eventually feels surrounded by the framework itself.Those concerns no longer look theoretical.Israel increasingly finds itself questioning arrangements involving countries that were supposed to help guarantee its security, while Iran – the country America set out to weaken decisively – is demonstrating that it can still impose enormous costs on the region.And Tehran understands the political clock.A senior IRGC adviser has openly discussed prolonging the confrontation until Trump is gone.Iran may have concluded that it does not need to defeat America militarily. It only needs to outlast Trump politically.Which brings us to the midterms. Is Washington simply trying to get through November?Reopen Hormuz. Stabilize oil prices. Remove Iran from the daily economic conversation. Replenish American weapons inventories. Get past the elections.Then perhaps Trump returns to Iran with overwhelming pressure.If that is the strategy, today's moves may eventually make sense.But Iran gets those same months. It can rebuild missiles, restore air defenses, receive Russian and Chinese equipment, strengthen proxies, repair military and nuclear infrastructure, and potentially do all of it with greater economic breathing room if Washington loosens sanctions.That is the gamble.Trump wanted to demonstrate American dominance without Israel participating in the second campaign.Instead, America today appears to be negotiating with the country it bombed over what that country must receive to stop disrupting global commerce.Maybe Trump has another card. Maybe this is a tactical pause before the real endgame.For America's sake, one hopes so.Because Trump's objectives were never merely to bomb Iran; they were to prevent a nuclear Iran, cripple its missile threat, cut its terrorist proxies off from Tehran, and restore American deterrence.Those are the standards by which victory must be measured.Not how many bombs America dropped. Not how many buildings were destroyed. And certainly not whether Iran temporarily agrees to reopen Hormuz after being economically rewarded for closing it.America took ownership of this second campaign. Now it must show the world what it accomplished.Because if Iran rebuilds, Hamas learns that agreements can be tested, America's regional partners increasingly organize around their own interests, and Washington pays Tehran to unwind a crisis Tehran helped create. The message then being sent across the Middle East will be exactly opposite the one Trump intended.And that leaves a question that would have seemed unimaginable when America's second attack began: Is Trump defeated – and is Iran victorious?The writer is founder and CEO of the Orthodox Jewish Chamber of Commerce.
news.author: Duvi Honig

news.title: "US-India relationship stronger than ever": Marco Rubio extends 80th Independence Day greetings
news.text: Washington, DC [US], August 15 (ANI): US Secretary of State Marco Rubio extended greetings to the people of India on the 80th Independence Day, saying the US-India relationship continues to grow and is "stronger than ever".In a statement issued on Friday (local time), Rubio said the relationship between US President Donald Trump and Prime Minister Narendra Modi had contributed to the growing ties between the two countries."On behalf of the United States of America, I extend warm congratulations to the people of India on their Independence Day. Thanks to the personal relationship between President Trump and Prime Minister Modi, the U.S.-India relationship continues to grow and is stronger than ever," Rubio said in a statement. The US Secretary of State highlighted cooperation between the two countries across several areas, including defence, energy security, critical minerals, artificial intelligence, space cooperation and commerce. He said the collaboration was making both nations, as well as the broader Indian Ocean region, "safer, stronger, and more prosperous"."From defence and energy security to critical minerals, artificial intelligence, space cooperation, and commerce, our collaboration is making both of our nations, and the broader Indian Ocean region, safer, stronger, and more prosperous," Rubip said. "The deep ties of friendship and family between our two peoples form the foundation of a partnership that is innovative, resilient, and forward-looking. The United States looks forward to the future our two countries will build together," he added. Earlier, the national flag was hoisted at the Indian High Commission in Canberra on Saturday (local time) as part of the 'Suryapath Tiranga' initiative to mark India's 80th Independence Day, which seeks to carry the Tricolour across the globe from one sunrise to the next.Prime Minister Narendra Modi will lead the 80th Independence Day celebrations at the Red Fort in Delhi on Saturday, with this year's event marking 150 years of the National Song 'Vande Mataram' and highlighting the role of 'Yuva Shakti' in India's journey towards Viksit Bharat 2047.For the first time, 'Vande Mataram' will be rendered during the Independence Day celebrations at the Red Fort.According to a press release, the Prime Minister will be received at the Red Fort by Defence Minister Rajnath Singh, Minister of State for Defence Sanjay Seth and Defence Secretary Rajesh Kumar Singh. He will then receive the Guard of Honour comprising personnel from the Army, Navy, Air Force and Delhi Police.Prime Minister Modi will proceed to the ramparts of the Red Fort, where he will hoist the National Flag. Captain Sonia Singh Chauhan will assist him in hoisting the Tricolour.The flag hoisting will be synchronised with a 21-gun salute by the 1721 Field Battery (Ceremonial), using indigenous 105 mm Light Field Guns, the press release stated.The Prime Minister will subsequently address the nation. This will mark PM Modi's 13th consecutive address from the ramparts of the Red Fort. At the conclusion of his speech, NCC cadets and 'My Bharat' volunteers will sing 'Vande Mataram', followed by the National Anthem.A total of 2,500 boy and girl cadets from the Army, Navy and Air Force, along with 'My Bharat' volunteers, will participate in the celebrations. They will be seated on Gyanpath and form the words 'Vande Mataram'. (ANI)

news.title: Map of Measles Cases Spiking as Trump Admin Overhauls Vaccine Advice
news.text: The U.S. measles map jumped again this week, with Wisconsin among the states seeing fresh outbreak‑linked cases as the Trump administration pushes a sweeping overhaul of childhood vaccine recommendations. The country is experiencing its highest measles caseload in more than three decades—colliding with a federal directive to split the long‑standing MMR shot into three separate injections. Families, pediatricians and state health systems face more appointments, shifting guidance and widening immunity gaps as vaccination rates fall and outbreaks accelerate. As of August 13, CDC data show 2,566 confirmed measles cases nationwide, including 38 new outbreaks this year—94 percent of all cases. Wisconsin is among the 47 jurisdictions reporting infections, with state immunization records showing a multi‑year decline in MMR coverage among young children. The administration’s new “Gold Standard Childhood Vaccine Recommendations,” signed by President Donald Trump, would further restructure how and when children receive vaccines, prompting concern from pediatric experts and state health officials. Newsweek has reached out to the White House for comment. List of States Where Measles Cases Have Been Reported CDC data shows 2,550 of the 2,566 cases occurred among U.S. residents, with infections confirmed in: Only 16 cases were reported among international visitors. The geographic spread mirrors declining MMR vaccination rates in many states, particularly in regions where kindergarten coverage has fallen below the 95 percent threshold needed for herd immunity. States with large outbreaks this year also overlap with areas where vaccine hesitancy has grown and where school-entry exemptions have increased. Wisconsin’s Measles Spike and the State’s Falling MMR Rates Wisconsin’s measles uptick comes as the state’s childhood vaccination rates continue to erode. According to the Wisconsin Immunization Registry, MMR coverage for 24‑month‑olds fell from 84.9 percent in 2019 to 79.8 percent in 2025, a drop that leaves thousands more children vulnerable to infection. Coverage among 6‑year‑olds—those expected to have completed the two‑dose MMR series—also slipped from 81.6 percent in 2019 to 75.3 percent in 2025. These declines matter because measles is one of the most contagious viruses on earth. CDC data show 93 percent of U.S. measles cases this year occurred in people who were unvaccinated or whose vaccination status was unknown. Wisconsin’s pockets of low coverage—particularly in counties such as Clark, Monroe, Vernon, and Crawford, where rates have dipped below 70 percent—create fertile ground for outbreaks. The CDC’s national map shows Wisconsin among states reporting between 10 and 49 cases, though the exact number is expected to shift as investigations continue. Health officials say most cases are linked to household clusters and exposure in community settings with low vaccination rates. How Vaccine Rates Changed—and Why Wisconsin Is Vulnerable Now The state’s downward trend began before the pandemic but accelerated afterward. Between 2020 and 2025, Wisconsin saw declines across nearly every childhood vaccine series, including DTaP, Hib, PCV and varicella. The MMR drop is particularly consequential because measles spreads through the air and can linger for hours. Public health officials point to several factors: Dr. Melissa Stockwell, Division Chief of Child and Adolescent Health at Columbia University, told Newsweek that splitting the MMR shot “adds unnecessary extra burden for families” and “raises the risk of missed and delayed doses, leaving the child unprotected for longer.” She warned that measles can cause pneumonia, encephalitis and other severe complications—risks that rise when children receive doses later than recommended. Dr. Patsy Stinchfield, Executive Director of the Measles Collaborative, told Newsweek that the combined MMR shot has been safely used since 1971 and that “more than 99 percent of people who receive two doses after their first birthday develop protective antibodies.” She called the administration’s plan to divide the shot “not an evidence‑based recommendation." Trump’s New Vaccine Schedule Collides With a National Measles Surge The administration’s executive order directs HHS to split the MMR vaccine into three separate shots—measles, mumps and rubella—once manufacturers can produce them domestically. It also encourages spacing out all childhood vaccines into separate appointments “to the maximum extent feasible.” The order moves several vaccines—including RSV monoclonal antibodies, hepatitis A and B, meningococcal B and ACWY—into a high‑risk category, narrowing routine access. It also instructs states to review school‑entry immunization laws and consider updates aligned with the new federal recommendations. Public health groups say the order is not grounded in new evidence. The Partnership to Fight Infectious Disease warned that rewriting vaccine guidance during the largest measles resurgence in decades “will only leave more American children vulnerable to preventable illness.” Sen. Bill Cassidy, a Louisiana Republican and physician, criticized the order, saying the president “does not have the expertise to make these changes” and warning that splitting the MMR shot would increase hesitancy and leave children exposed longer. Are Individual MMR Shots Available? What States and Manufacturers Say Despite the administration’s directive, single‑antigen measles, mumps and rubella vaccines are not currently available in the United States. Manufacturers have not announced plans to produce them, and pediatric experts say there is “little incentive” to create separate products. The CDC’s vaccine schedule, updated monthly, has not changed since the executive order. The agency continues to recommend the combined MMR shot at 12–15 months and 4–6 years. When asked why the schedule has not been updated, CDC officials said they are reviewing the order and awaiting HHS guidance. State health departments—including Wisconsin DHS—continue to advise families to follow the existing CDC schedule, citing the ongoing outbreak and the high effectiveness of the combined MMR vaccine. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Samantha Beech and Gray R. Thomas
news.summary: U.S. measles cases hit 2,566 as outbreaks surge nationwide, with 94% linked to ongoing transmission.

news.title: Funding Uncertainty Could Slow Pentagon’s Golden Dome Program, General Says
news.text:
The Pentagon’s Golden Dome space-based missile defense system is at risk of being delayed if Congress can’t figure out how to continue funding the program, Space Force Gen. Mike Guetlein said Aug. 11.

“If they don’t figure it out, there is no Golden Dome because there is no funding,” Guetlein told audience members at the annual Space and Missile Defense Symposium in Huntsville, Alabama, according to Defense Daily.

The Pentagon has funded the program through budget reconciliation since it was first launched by President Donald Trump in 2025.

The multilayered defense system is designed to protect the United States from aerial threats, including complex ballistic, cruise, and hypersonic missiles.

The Department of War is funding the Golden Dome through a $25 billion allocation in the 2025 reconciliation bill but needs continued funding for operations if they want to meet a 2028 deadline set by Trump, Guetlein told reporters at the symposium.

“As a nation, we’re going to figure this out just because the sense of urgency is so great,” Guetlein said. “It is a tough situation that we find ourselves in as a nation.”

The program also cleared another hurdle Aug. 11 with a successful test of weapons technologies at White Sands Missile Range in New Mexico.

SpaceX, Northrop Grumman Corp., and other companies involved in a $185 billion initiative successfully completed the first round of critical tests for space-based missile interceptors, Guetlein said.

The companies will now move into the next phase, which involved demonstrating the technologies’ capabilities in space.

Some members of Congress have argued against funding the program, raising concerns about the viability of the technology.

Sen. Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.) questioned the reliability of the dome system and said it had problems with cost reliability.

“We need some confidence that the system is going to deliver the capability that’s being promised. And to me, right now, it’s clear that it won’t,” Kelly said July 15 during a Senate Armed Services Committee hearing. “The most ambitious elements of Golden Dome is the space-based interceptor layer and that is going to face significant technical challenges.

“The cost, the physics, the likely reliability, in my view, do not support a full-scale space-based intercept architecture,” Kelly said. “This means that we could spend more than a trillion dollars and end up with a system that doesn’t work and does’t meaningful improve our security.”

The threat of an attack in North America is real, Guetlein said.

“The adversary has been watching the way we fight and they have become very determined to counter us in many different domains,” Guetlein told the audience. “But worse yet they’ve become very capable and very determined in doing that. That includes holding the homeland at risk. It has come to point that we’ve got to address those threats, and that’s what the Golden Dome is going to go after.”

Gen. Gregory Guillot, U.S. Air Force Commander of the Northern Command and North American Aerospace Defense Command described the heightened threat environment in February 2025.

“Today, our competitors have the capability and capacity to threaten all of North America with a range of advanced nuclear, conventional, and non-kinetic systems while employing disruptive grey-zone, cyber, and information operations against the United States and our international partners,” Guillot told the Senate Armed Services Committee.

Strategic cooperation between the United States’ four main adversaries—Iran, Russia, North Korea, and China—has grown since the beginning of the Ukraine War, increasing the likelihood of a direct conflict with the United States, the general said.

news.title: LA Olympics has to allow politicians on the bus, just not behind the wheel - Coe
news.text: The London Olympics in 2012 are widely credited with being one of the best prepared and managed Summer Games in recent history and their organiser Sebastian Coe is urging LA28 organisers to work as closely with government as he did. Coe, the man who delivered the London Games as head of the local organising committee, says the organisers of the Los Angeles Olympics in two years' time will have to accept working shoulder-to-shoulder with the US administration. "I know it's really important that you have really good working relationships with government, prime ministers," said Coe, who is now head of track and field's governing body World Athletics. The United States have just co-hosted the Football World Cup, but there were concerns raised throughout the tournament over the relationship between US President Donald Trump and FIFA head Gianni Infantino. Infantino, a Swiss-Italian who has led FIFA since 2016, was a frequent visitor to the White House in the buildup to the World Cup. Last year he awarded Trump a newly-created and much-mocked FIFA peace prize, which he presented to the president at the World Cup draw in Washington. Infantino was then forced into defending the decision to reprieve US World Cup star Folarin Balogun after Trump said he had appealed directly to the head of world football's governing body over the issue. Balogun, the US team's outstanding player at the World Cup, had been set to miss the last-16 game against Belgium after receiving a red card in the victory over Bosnia-Herzegovina in the previous round. But FIFA said it was suspending the card, allowing Balogun to play against Belgium, sparking a furore. Trump said he had called Infantino "because I didn't think it was a foul". President Trump will still be in power by the time of the LA Games in July 2028. - Politics with small 'p' - Coe told journalists at the European championships on Thursday that the local organising committee of the LA Olympics had to strike a balance with the US government. "The delivery of the Games is in large part predicated on those relationships with Treasury, Defense, Homeland Security," Coe said of the relevant government ministries in the US. "Actually the best mitigation against risk at a Games is the relationships that you have politically, and I mean with a small 'P', in the system. "No local organising committee can make the Games safe. That is done with a combination of intelligence services." External interference, Coe argued, comes "entirely down to the resilience of a sporting organisation to say, 'Yeah, I hear what you say, but thank you and good night'. "The balance is keeping the politicians on the bus, but not letting them anywhere near the steering wheel. "I probably achieved that quite well in London." Coe added: "That's entirely about the resilience and robust nature of your sport. Casey Wasserman is head of the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics organising committee (768x512, AR: 1.50)"But not having those relationships is dangerous." Former Zimbabwean swimmer Kirsty Coventry beat Coe in last year's election to succeed Thomas Bach as the new president of the International Olympic Committee. On taking over as Olympic chief, Coventry was asked about the prospect of dealing with President Trump. "I have been dealing with let's say difficult men in high positions since I was 20 years old," she answered. More recently, Coventry expressed confidence that the Los Angeles Olympics organisers and IOC would be able to overcome a number of the challenges that shook the World Cup, notably visa issues. That, she said, took "consistent collaboration and learning". "We have to just continue having faith in that process. And I do believe that we will see a successful LA 2028." lp/gj

news.title: World News | 62 Commercial Vessels Redirected, Three Disabled Amid US Blockade on Iran: CENTCOM
news.text:
Washington, DC [US], August 15 (ANI): The US Central Command (CENTCOM) said on Friday (local time) that its forces had redirected 62 commercial vessels, disabled three, and boarded two others while enforcing the US blockade against Iran in the Arabian Sea.

CENTCOM stated that the actions were taken to ensure compliance with the blockade.

Also Read | Australia Social Media Ban: Tech Giants Urge Caution Over Early Data As Penalties Rise To AUD 99 Million.

"A US Sailor directs an MH-60R Sea Hawk helicopter during nighttime flight operations aboard the guided-missile cruiser USS Princeton (CG 59) as the ship sails in the Arabian Sea and enforces the U.S. blockade against Iran. As of Aug. 14, CENTCOM forces have redirected 62 commercial vessels, disabled 3 and boarded 2 to ensure compliance," CENTCOM said.

The development comes amid ongoing tensions between the US and Iran as both countries continue to stake claims of control over the Strait of Hormuz.

Also Read | Luigi Mangione Pleads Guilty in UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson Killing: What Charges Does He Face?.

On Thursday, US War Secretary Pete Hegseth warned that the United States would continue its naval blockade on Iranian ports "indefinitely" and for as long as needed, as reported by Al Jazeera.

Speaking to reporters in Panama City, Hegseth emphasised that the US Navy can keep the blockade in place by rotating ships in and out of the region as required.

"Indefinitely, the United States Navy can maintain a blockade like that because we'll rotate ships in and out, as we have, and we'll continue to," he said.

US President Donald Trump claimed that the United States exercised "total control" over the Strait of Hormuz and that he "will keep it" amid stalled negotiations with Iran regarding the reopening of the strategic conduit. Trump asserted, "The USA has total control over the Strait of Hormuz. I THINK WE WILL KEEP IT! Our Naval Blockade is being called, by everyone, 'A WALL OF STEEL,' and there is nothing Iran can do about it."

Trump further maintained that Tehran's military infrastructure had been severely degraded, concluding his message with, "Praise be to Allah!"

"All they have is FAKE NEWS and 300 per cent INFLATION, and it's getting worse! Iran is all talk and no action, and is the Bully of the Middle East No Longer. Praise be to Allah!" he added in the social media post.

However, soon after Trump's remarks, Iran rejected his claims, stating that the strategic waterway remains blocked and will not be reopened until Tehran's conditions are accepted.

The Persian Gulf Strait Authority said Trump's claims and repeated statements by US officials that the Strait of Hormuz was no longer blocked did not change the situation.

"Claims and repeated posts by US officials that the Strait of Hormuz is no longer blocked do not change the reality: the Strait of Hormuz remains blocked and will not be reopened until Iran's conditions are accepted," the PGSA said.

The Strait of Hormuz remains one of the world's most sensitive geopolitical chokepoints, where past military standoffs have routinely triggered spikes in international crude prices and fears of broader conflict. The current escalation has already prompted expanded naval patrols, adjustments to shipping routes by commercial carriers, and renewed international calls for diplomatic restraint.

Commercial shipping through the vital corridor currently continues under tight security oversight, though the environment remains highly volatile. Immediate diplomatic attention remains centred on whether negotiations can yield a temporary truce to mitigate the likelihood of armed conflict while keeping maritime trade routes open. (ANI)

news.title: Iran defiant on strait as Trump tells Americans to accept high gas prices
news.text:
CAIRO/GARDEN CITY, New York, Aug 15 - Iran called on the U.S. to accept defeat while President Donald Trump blasted Iran as "evil" and urged Americans to brace for continued high fuel prices.

The comments suggested the warring parties remained far apart, with progress toward peace talks and oil tanker traffic through the strategic Strait of Hormuz waterway both halted.

"This strait will be opened and closed only under Iran's command, and so long as you do not accept the reality of defeat and stop indulging in fantasies, Iran will continue to enforce the blockade," Iran's Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi said in a post on X early Saturday, showing little urgency toward restoring prewar trade.

"The Strait of Hormuz cannot be seized by a tweet or an aircraft carrier, by issuing an order or by delivering an election speech," he said.

One out of every five barrels of the world's oil exports passed through the strait before the U.S. and Israel launched the war on February 28.

Trump on Friday urged Americans to accept slightly higher gasoline prices while the conflict with Iran continues.

At a political rally in Garden City, New York, Trump said paying "a tiny little bit more for your gasoline" is worth the cost of ensuring "a very evil country" could not have a nuclear weapon, one of the president's stated rationales for the war.

In a trend that has fueled inflation and disappointed voters, the average U.S. price of a gallon of gasoline was about $4.08 on Friday, according to the American Automobile Association. That's up 29% from $3.16 a year earlier.

Only two vessels passed through the Strait of Hormuz on Friday, according to analysis from ship-tracking firm Kpler: a grain ship entering Iranian waters and an empty dry bulk ship going the other direction. A separate empty liquefied petroleum products tanker was sailing into the Gulf via the strait, the data showed. There were no crude oil shipments visible.

Some ships may cross the strait undetected with their transponders off, but the figures are nowhere near the more than 130 ships that traversed it daily before the war.

Those that dare navigate the strait without Iranian permission risk missile or drone strikes. The United Arab Emirates' Abu Dhabi National Oil Company said two of its vessels were attacked transiting the strait on Thursday evening, then the Emirati state news agency WAM reported another vessel came under attack on Friday.

Iran labels its enforcement of strait traffic a blockade, while the U.S. uses the same term for its threat against Iranian vessels leaving their ports.

"What we're doing is a great service for the world, not only for ourselves ... and we're really doing a great job," Trump said, adding that a 260-day deployment by a U.S. aircraft carrier supporting the war effort was "not nearly long enough."

With a tentative June deal to end the war in tatters, there was no sign that the U.S. or Iran planned to resume peace talks.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi said no decision has yet been made to restart negotiations with the United States, the Iranian Student News Agency reported on Saturday. Mediators Qatar and Pakistan were in contact with Iran and exchanging messages, but this did not amount to negotiations, the agency said.

ECONOMIC TOLL

Higher fuel prices have collided with a Trump campaign promise to lower energy costs, and Democrats are seeking to make economic fallout of the Iran war an issue in the November midterm elections.

The virtual closure of the strait helped raise crude oil futures another $1 a barrel on Friday. Benchmark Brent and West Texas Intermediate futures were on track for weekly gains of 6.0% and 5.4%, respectively.

Gharibabadi said Tehran would not be intimidated by threats or a show of force. But there were signs of an economic toll on Iran.

In remarks broadcast on state television, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian blamed high inflation on a U.S. blockade of Iranian ports and sanctions on Iran's oil exports.

Trump and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent each pledged to inflict more financial damage on Iran. Bessent told Newsmax's "Rob Schmitt Tonight" program on Thursday that announcements of more measures against Iran were coming next week.

The latest attacks by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis renewed concerns about a widening regional war. Yemen's internationally recognized government said the Houthis fired six ballistic missiles at the Red Sea port of Mocha on Friday, killing four civilians.

Separately, the Houthi-run SABA news agency cited a military source as saying the group had targeted an Aramco facility in the Saudi city of Najran with a drone. REUTERS

news.title: BBC wants to interview Jared and Ivanka Trump as part of its defense in Trump defamation lawsuit
news.text:
The BBC is seeking to subpoena the president’s children, Donald Trump Jr. and Ivanka Trump, as well as his son-in-law Jared Kushner, as part of the Republican’s ongoing defamation suit against the broadcaster.

In a Friday filing in Florida federal court, the BBC argued that the trio “without question have personal knowledge” about President Trump’s mindset surrounding his speech the day of the January 6, 2021, Capitol riot.

The $10 billion suit, filed in late 2025, alleges the BBC used misleading editing in a 2024 documentary to splice together disparate parts of the speech and make it sound like Trump was calling for violence, when in fact he told demonstrators to peacefully head to the Capitol.

The broadcaster has apologized for the edit but argues the president doesn’t have grounds to bring the suit.

The BBC argues that subpoenaing Kushner and the Trumps would help explain the president’s thinking around the speech, ultimately helping answer what the president meant by his remarks and whether the documentary meaningfully altered his message.

Trump Jr. and Ivanka Trump were in the Oval Office on January 6 with the president as he revised the speech, then subsequently watched him deliver it from the Ellipse, shortly before the Capitol riot, according to testimony from the January 6 committee in Congress.

Ivanka Trump remained with the president after the speech, while both Trump Jr. and Kushner advised the White House and its allies on how to respond to the escalating violence at the Capitol. 

The Friday filing claims security around the Trumps has prevented the BBC from serving them with subpoenas.

“Law enforcement officers” stopped the BBC from serving Ivanka Trump and Kushner at their home, directing the broadcaster to coordinate with the Secret Service, which then claimed it couldn’t accept the documents on their behalf, the BBC alleges.

A similar scene allegedly played out at Trump Tower, where security stopped the subpoena from being delivered, the BBC claims.

The president’s legal team also allegedly rejected an attempt to serve Kushner and the Trumps through him, the BBC alleges.

The Independent has contacted the president’s lawyers, the Trump Organization and the Secret Service for comment.

Last month, a federal judge ruled that President Trump must provide detailed information about his companies’ finances as part of the lawsuit, though the court later temporarily paused that request.
news.summary: The broadcaster argues the Trump family was close to president as he worked on infamous January 6 speech at heart of the case

news.title: BBC seeks to subpoena Trump's family members in Panorama lawsuit
news.text:
BBC seeks to subpoena Trump's family members in Panorama lawsuit

The BBC has sought to subpoena members of Donald Trump's family for documents and testimony as it defends against the US president's $10bn (£7.4bn) defamation lawsuit against the broadcaster.

Court filings show that representatives for the BBC's legal team attempted in May to serve subpoenas to the president's son Donald Trump Jr., his daughter Ivanka Trump and son-in-law Jared Kushner.

The president is suing the BBC over an episode of Panorama that edited together two different sections of a speech he gave before the 2021 Capitol riots. 

The BBC has previously apologised for the edit but denied it was grounds for defamation.

In the latest filing, the BBC's lawyers argue Trump's family members "have personal knowledge" of his intentions in delivering the speech, making their testimony and documents relevant to the president's defamation claim. 

Drawing on evidence previously gathered by a US congressional committee, the filing says Donald Trump Jr and Ivanka Trump were present when their father revised and delivered his speech, adding Jared Kushner drafted a proposed statement for him which would have condemned the use of violence.

The filing asks the court to allow the subpoenas to be served by email and certified mail, saying attempts to serve them by hand were unsuccessful. 

In one instance, according to the document, a representative for the BBC's legal team tried to deliver a subpoena for Ivanka Trump and Jared Kushner at their home in Florida, but was refused entry at a police checkpoint and was later told by the Secret Service that the agency could not accept the subpoenas. 

Similarly, according to the filing, a representative tried to serve a subpoena for Donald Trump Jr at Trump Tower in New York but was told by the concierge that the person who normally takes such documents may be at lunch. 

During another attempt two days later, the representative was told the "legal department" was not in that day, according to the filing.

President Trump's legal team has been approached for comment. The BBC press office declined to comment.

Last December, Trump sued the BBC and subsidiaries BBC Studios Productions and BBC Studios Distribution over the 2024 Panorama episode.

Trump's lawsuit - filed in Florida - accuses the BBC of "intentionally, maliciously, and deceptively doctoring" the speech he gave outside the Capitol on 6 January 2021.

The BBC has apologised for an editing error that gave "the mistaken impression that President Trump had made a direct call for violent action".

However, the BBC has asked the court to dismiss the lawsuit, arguing that the programme doesn't meet the legal criteria for defamation and wasn't made available on its US platforms.

Last month, Trump's lawyers admitted they had no evidence that the documentary was available in the US on the BBC's BritBox subscription service, as they had originally claimed, or on BBC.com, BBC Select or through US broadcasters.

Trump also recently agreed to drop the BBC's commercial arm BBC Studios from his lawsuit, after the BBC argued the company had "no role in creating or producing the documentary".

Earlier this month, the judge in the case granted Trump's request for a delay in him handing over a financial documents to the broadcaster as part of the suit. 

The BBC has asked for some of Trump's financial records in relation to his argument that the documentary damaged the president's business interests. 

The president's legal team said disclosure of the financial records would cause him "irreparable harm".

A trial date in February 2027 has been scheduled, should the case progress.

news.title: GENERAL SIR RICHARD SHIRREFF: Why I believe this charming Arctic island is where Putin could start WWIII
news.text:
On Spitsbergen there are so many polar bears that it’s against the law to leave town without carrying a gun.

The only inhabited island in the Svalbard archipelago, Spitsbergen is Norwegian territory.

But 30 miles from its capital, Longyearbyen (population 2,000), lies the town of Barentsburg, which is home to a community of Russian miners.

There the Moscow-owned Arktikugol company oversees a desultory coal-mining operation. The coal it produces is poor quality, and the cost of extracting it high, but the mine provides an invaluable excuse for the Kremlin to maintain a unique toehold within a Western sovereign territory.

And in the months and years to come I predict that this obscure Arctic outcrop, 800 miles south of the North Pole, will play a key role in Russia’s plan to destabilise the Nato alliance.

Spitsbergen may be a burgeoning tourist destination – it has its own annual music festival – but it could also serve as the flashpoint that sparks World War III.

Steady on General, I hear you say. But we only have to look back at the recent history of Russian aggression to see how such a disaster could play out.

Before the annexation of Crimea in 2014 and the invasion of Ukraine eight years later, Vladimir Putin staged attacks by mercenaries and special forces against Russians living in those regions. He then declared that, to protect these people, he had no option but to order military intervention.

This is just the sort of justification he will use for seizing Spitsbergen. He will claim Russian miners are under attack by their Norwegian neighbours and need protection.

To make the lie more credible, and to give his armies of social media trolls some material to help give credibility to their fake reports, he will make sure the miners really do come under attack.

And on a frontier Arctic island where everyone has a gun, some will probably be killed.

A small, well-rehearsed, Russian airborne operation, involving special and maritime forces will take control of Spitsbergen within a few hours and martial law will be imposed immediately.

The question then is – what does Nato do?

The simmering conflict between Nato and Russia is now at its most volatile for decades. Last week, after a drone laden with Semtex explosives was discovered close to a cargo plane at Germany’s Leipzig airport, Western surveillance sources warned that Russia is planning a series of attacks to test Nato’s resolve.

This echoes warnings from the American intelligence network to their counterparts in Britain’s security services earlier this month that the Baltic states are under threat.

Putin is not bluffing. With his back to the wall after more than four years of war in Ukraine, and with domestic discontent growing, he is desperate for ways to cling to power.

Full-on war with Europe will help him in two ways – by undermining our determination to support Ukraine and by uniting the Russian people against a common enemy, Nato.

The Baltic countries, which share a 600-mile border with Russia and its vassal state Belarus, are understandably nervous.

Lithuanian defence minister Robertas Kaunas warned this week that Moscow is planning ‘false flag’ attacks, to make it appear as though Ukraine is committing terrorist acts in Europe.

‘We have data that Russia is considering conducting unconventional kinetic attacks on critical infrastructure in the Baltic region,’ he says. ‘It is likely that Russia could use Ukrainian-made drones for this purpose.’

That tallies with the incident at Leipzig airport on August 4: the drone armed with high explosives appeared to be Ukrainian, but it was almost certainly planted by Russia.

An Antonov cargo plane packed with ammunition bound for Kyiv was parked nearby and only a faulty detonator in the sabotage drone prevented a huge explosion that could have caused a devastating loss of life.

Meanwhile, two men believed to be in the pay of Russia – Ukrainian national Roman Lavrynovych 22, and Ukrainian-born Romanian national Stanislav Carpiuc, 27 – were jailed in June for arson attacks on a house and a car linked to Sir Keir Starmer, while he was Prime Minister.

Last month, during a bombardment of Ukrainian targets, a Russian cruise missile overshot the border and crashed into a field 50 miles inside Poland.

All this evidence of Putin’s intention to provoke war with Nato is backed up by satellite images released in June that show a Russian military build-up at five strategic points along its borders with the West.

Tracts of forest are being razed for a base at Petsjenga, high above the Arctic Circle, 110 miles northwest of the strategically important port of Murmansk and just seven miles from the Norwegian border.

Around 4,000 Russian troops are already based there, but new barracks are under construction that could accommodate 10,000.

About 375 miles to the south, at Kandalaksha on the border with Finland, a base is being built to house an artillery brigade. The chief of Finland’s defence intelligence service, Major General Pekka Turunen, has warned that since his country joined Nato in 2023, Russia has increased its military presence along the border.

The same is true in Kaliningrad, the Russian enclave on the Baltic coast between Lithuania and Poland, and on the border with Estonia.

When I wrote my novel 2017: War With Russia a decade ago, I believed the most likely trigger point was in the Baltic states.

It was all too plausible that Russia would engineer a series of ‘false flag’ attacks, blaming Nato forces for atrocities they themselves carried out, such as the killing of Russian-speaking demonstrators in Latvia by snipers.

Putin will be counting on dissent and panic among the Western allies in response to whatever incursion he finally settles on.

It will be a serious test of Nato’s resolve and one he expects us to fail. And he will be right, at least in part.

It seems highly unlikely that the United States will honour its obligation under Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty, a promise it made in 1949 to treat any attack on one Nato country as an attack on all member countries.

I predict that President Donald Trump will refuse to send troops to assist in any military operation to rescue Spitsbergen. He might well crow about it and claim that Russia would never have dared act if Greenland had been ceded to the US, as he demanded last year. Europe refused to give up territory then, and now – he is likely to say – Europe must pay the price.

He is already badly letting down the Ukrainian cause. This week there was an intriguing development in Russo-US relations when a former US Marine called Robert Gilman, who had been arrested while travelling through southwestern Russia by train a month before the invasion of Ukraine, was returned to the US.

He has spent the last four and a half years in a Russian jail after being charged with drunkenness and assaulting a police officer and his family say he was in poor health due to the cruel treatment he was subjected to by his captors.

Trump framed his release as a diplomatic masterstroke, saying: ‘Russia asked for no one in return – no exchange took place.’

To which the only logical response has to be: pull the other one Donald.

So what was Russia’s price? One rumoured possibility is that the Kremlin extracted a promise from Washington that it would turn down Ukraine’s request to allow it to manufacture Patriot missiles, its best hope of bolstering its air defences against ballistic missile attacks.

Kyiv has never been in more dire need of interceptor missiles. With its stocks now virtually entirely depleted, the citizens of Ukraine’s capital are living in terror of nightly attacks.

I have many friends there, and one of them told me last week she is more frightened than at any time since Putin’s demented war began.

Russia is firing ballistic missiles at both Kyiv and Zaporizhzhia, 350 miles to the southeast, targeting civilian buildings with psychotic ruthlessness in a bid to destroy Ukrainian morale.

These supersonic rockets fall from outside the Earth’s atmosphere and can be travelling at more than 5,000mph by the time they make impact.

Such is their speed – one commentator described them as arriving in the time it takes to deliver a pizza – that the residents of these cities often have just five minutes’ warning, at best.

Sometimes the first they know of an attack is when a missile explodes. The carnage they cause is colossal.

But America has used up such vast quantities of munitions in its disastrous war on Iran that there is no hope that the US will supply Patriots to Kyiv. It simply has none to spare.

Ukraine’s only hope in the short term is for other Nato nations with Patriots to give what they can while Trump grants it a licence to manufacture them.

But, as we have seen, this prospect is looking more unlikely than ever.

We cannot count on his support against a Russian incursion in the Arctic either.

Nor can we be sure that every other Nato country would stand shoulder to shoulder with Norway. Hungary’s commitment to the alliance is untested since Peter Magyar ousted long-time president Viktor Orban – a friend of Putin – earlier this year.

Portugal, Spain and Italy are all struggling with a surge of illegal migration that leaves little room to deal with other crises.

All those countries, our long-term allies, would be justified in accusing the UK of lacking visible commitment too.

Since Andy Burnham became Prime Minister a month ago, he has said next to nothing about defence.

Labour’s most prominent advocate of re-arming, former Defence Secretary John Healey, is now the Chancellor of the Exchequer – an appointment that has had the effect, incidental or not, of making it much harder for him to argue that Britain urgently needs to increase its defence spending. He’s now the man who has to balance the books.

I am utterly certain that, if Russia does invade Spitsbergen – or stage any other land grab – Britain will be at the forefront of the Nato response.

Norway is a valued friend of Britain and our Commando forces train constantly with their Norwegian counterparts, and our Arctic warfare units are among the best in the world.

But I’m also deeply concerned that, in a shooting war with Russia, we will suffer badly.

We do not have the air defences, the naval forces, the ammunition, the military reserves or anything else needed to ward off attack.

At least one Russian warship is now constantly stationed off the British coast. Russian drones, probably launched from trawlers, have buzzed our RAF bases, photographing every inch of them.

We are desperately vulnerable. Britain will never shirk its duty to support its Nato allies.

But we have relinquished much of our ability to defend our own cities and our own people.

Putin is looking for an excuse to start a war with us and is making no secret of it.

If he succeeds in his aim of provoking Nato into a chaotic, ill-coordinated war, the destruction and loss of life we have seen in Ukraine could well be inflicted on Britain too.

General Sir Richard Shirreff is former Deputy Supreme Allied Commander Europe, Nato

news.title: Poll: Voters lean ‘no’ on California voter ID measure, split on billionaire tax
news.text:
A poll released Friday by UC Berkeley’s Institute of Governmental Studies shows voters aren’t sold on a proposed billionaire tax or a voter ID initiative set to appear on their ballots this November.

The poll found that 48% of likely voters would support Proposition 40, a proposed one-time, 5% tax on the assets of billionaires, while 41% said they would vote against it. Eleven percent remained undecided.

The poll of 4,207 registered voters found that a majority — 51% — plan to vote against Prop. 39, a constitutional amendment that would require voters to furnish government-issued ID before casting a ballot; 42% said they plan on voting “yes” on the measure.

That’s a problem for backers of both measures, particularly months out from the election, according to IGS Poll Director Mark DiCamillo.

“Usually undecided voters tend to break toward the ‘no’ side because it doesn’t change anything,” DiCamillo said. “It’s a status quo kind of vote.”

Both proposals show sharp partisan divides. The poll found that seven out of 10 Democrats back the wealth tax, while 80% of Republicans reject it. Half of independent voters said they support the measure, compared to 39% opposed.

Prop. 39 shows the opposite dynamic, with Republicans overwhelmingly backing the voter ID requirement and all but 12% of Democrats saying they plan to vote against it. A majority — 54% — of independents said they also will vote against Prop. 39.

The poll complicates a key argument for the largely conservative backers of Prop. 39, who’ve pitched it as a commonsense, bipartisan policy with broad support across the political spectrum. Opponents have cast it as part of President Donald Trump's false claims of election fraud.

The billionaire tax, which would funnel revenue toward healthcare services facing steep federal cuts pushed by Trump, shows sharp age divides. Three-quarters of voters under 30 support the tax, but support drops by age bracket and bottoms out among voters 65 and older, with 40% supporting the tax. That could present difficulties for SEIU-United Healthworkers West, the union driving the tax, because younger voters generally are less likely to turn out than older ones.

The poll was commissioned by the Los Angeles Times and was conducted Aug. 3-9, in the midst of two key Prop. 40 endorsements. The California Democratic Party backed the tax on Aug. 2, and the Labor Federation of California endorsed it several days later.

Support for Prop. 40 is highest among lower income voters rather than higher earners, stronger among Black and Latino voters, at 60%, compared to white voters, at 40%, and higher among women, 53%, than men, 42%.

news.title: Yemen’s government says Houthi attack on al-Makha kills at least four  - Antigua Tribune – Daily Antigua
news.text:
The Houthis have launched an attack on the Red Sea port city of al-Makha (Mocha), killing at least four people, Yemen’s internationally recognised government says.

The government said the Houthis ⁠fired six ballistic ⁠missiles at al-Makha on Friday, amid an escalation in hostilities between the Iran-aligned group and its Saudi-backed opponents.

The armed forces aligned with the Yemeni government said the attack targeted civilian infrastructure and national assets at the port, adding that initial reports said four civilians were killed and several fishing boats were set on fire.

news.title: Trump finds new way to put name on Kennedy Center – media
news.text:
The Kennedy Center board has voted to restore Donald Trump’s name to the Washington arts venue, multiple media outlets have reported, just two months after it was removed on a federal judge’s orders.

The Trump-aligned board voted last December to rename the institution after Trump and John F. Kennedy, and his name was subsequently added to its facade. US District Judge Christopher Cooper ruled in May that the board lacked authority to change the name established by Congress and ordered the Trump signage removed. Workers complied in June.

This time, however, the board is not formally renaming the Kennedy Center after Trump. According to Axios, an inscription below the Kennedy Center sign will read “Restored and Renovated by President Donald J. Trump,” while the physical site will be named “the President Donald J. Trump Plaza.”

The new formulation puts Trump’s name back on the building without formally declaring that the Kennedy Center is named after him, apparently seeking to sidestep the restriction that only Congress can change the institution’s name.

The board also voted Thursday to move forward with a two-year closure of the center’s main venue for renovations. The proposed overhaul would refurbish aging infrastructure, polish the building’s marble facade, and renovate its halls and theaters.

“Under President Trump’s bold leadership, the Kennedy Center is on its way to becoming the finest cultural institution anywhere in the world,” White House spokeswoman Liz Huston told Axios.

The naming saga has already inspired legislation in Congress. In January, Senator Bernie Sanders and several Democratic colleagues introduced the Stop Executive Renaming for Vanity and Ego (SERVE) Act, which would prohibit federal buildings, land and other assets from being named after a sitting president. The bill remains at the committee stage.

Huston argued at the time that such naming efforts reflect policy achievements rather than branding, citing initiatives including the TrumpRx prescription drug website and noting that both Washington, DC and the Hoover Dam were named after presidents while they were still in office.

The Kennedy Center has reportedly found a way to restore Donald Trump’s name after it was removed on a federal judge’s orders

news.title: US regulator approves bank charter for Trump-backed crypto company World Liberty Financial
news.text:
Aug 14 (Reuters) - A national U.S. bank regulator on ⁠Friday conditionally approved a bank charter application linked to President Donald Trump and his family’s crypto venture, World Liberty Financial, effectively greenlighting an expansion of its stablecoin operations.

The Office of the ⁠Comptroller of the Currency said in a letter published on its website that it has granted conditional preliminary approval of World Liberty Trust Company’s application for a national trust charter, ‌which it applied for in January.

The charter, if ultimately approved at a later date, would allow World Liberty, through the newly created trust bank, to manage and hold assets on behalf of customers and settle payments faster. It does not generally permit deposit-taking or lending like traditional banks.

Hoping to capitalize on the Trump administration’s crypto-friendly stance, the industry has been knocking on the OCC’s door for such charters. They allow crypto companies to hold assets on behalf of clients nationwide under a single federal charter, as well as ​to provide other settlement and asset servicing functions — making it easier to court major institutional clients.

Other crypto firms, including Ripple and Circle, ⁠have received preliminary approval for such charters under Comptroller Jonathan Gould, whom Trump ⁠appointed to the role last year.

In the case of World Liberty, the charter would allow it to directly issue its USD1 stablecoin, as well as custody the U.S. dollar assets backing it, both of ⁠which ‌are now handled by a business partner, BitGo.

In a statement on Friday, the firm welcomed the conditional approval, calling it a "milestone" in its efforts to open the bank.

"A national trust bank brings USD1 issuance, custody, and reserve management together under OCC supervision, examined on the same standards that have governed banks for generations. We welcome continuous scrutiny from Federal regulators for many years to come," Zach Witkoff, World Liberty Trust ⁠president and chairman, said in a statement.

As in most cases, the charter is subject to conditions, including notifying the ​regulator of any major business plan changes, maintaining at least $20 million ‌in capital and hiring a qualified employee to serve as the firm's internal audit manager.

In its approval letter, the OCC noted it had received comments raising concerns about non-U.S. investors in ⁠World Liberty Financial.

The regulator said such ​investors were not considered principal shareholders in the bank, adding that the OCC had received so-called "passivity agreements" from several bank investors, including those outside the U.S., who vowed that they would not seek to control or influence the bank's operations or decisions.

Among the signatories on those agreements was Eric Trump, the president's son, as president of a Trump-family affiliated investment vehicle.

In February, two Democratic members of the U.S. Senate Banking Committee asked Trump's Treasury secretary to examine the potential national security implications of ⁠a reported purchase of a $500 million stake in World Liberty Financial in a deal linked with the United Arab ​Emirates' national security adviser.

FIRM HAS TIES TO TRUMP ALLIES

World Liberty Trust’s leadership is deeply intertwined with Trump's longtime allies,the Witkoff family.

Zach Witkoff is the son of Trump’s special diplomatic envoy, Steve Witkoff. The Witkoffs were among the co-founders of World Liberty Financial with Trump and his three sons in late 2024, with Zach Witkoff currently serving as its CEO.

Steve Witkoff’s brother Robert Witkoff, a former insurance company executive, will be a director of World Liberty ⁠Trust. Another proposed director, Scott Alper, is the president of the Witkoff family’s real estate business.

The OCC is part of the Treasury Department and unlike many other financial regulators does not have a bipartisan board.

Democrats have said a World Liberty charter would pose a major conflict of interest, and pressured Gould during a February congressional hearing to confidentially share the company's unredacted application. The public version did not include full details on its capital structure or business plans.

In its approval letter, the OCC said Gould and staff "acted consistently with their statutory duties and ethical obligations with respect to the application," adding the application was reviewed by career staff and the bank ​would similarly be supervised by nonpolitical examiners.

LUCRATIVE BUSINESS

World Liberty is the most prominent among the Trump family’s stable of lucrative crypto ventures. Its stated vision ⁠is to democratize finance, allowing anyone to bypass a traditional banking system that the Trumps have characterized as restrictive and unfair.

World Liberty has promoted the USD1 stablecoin as a flagship product that is designed to be a safe, ​U.S. dollar-backed asset allowing for entry to a range of financial products on the blockchain.

USD1 has grown quickly since being announced in March ‌2025. It is currently the fourth largest stablecoin by market capitalization, at around $4 billion.

Reuters estimated that the ​Trump family earned about $50 million from the USD1 stablecoin to the end of June 2026.

Overall, World Liberty Financial funneled more than $1.6 billion to the U.S. president and his family as of April, according to Reuters calculations.

news.title: Exclusive | China rattled by Trump White House chaos weeks ahead of Xi visit. It has happened before
news.text:
Just months ago, disorganised planning from Washington in the lead-up to President Donald Trump’s landmark China visit frustrated Chinese officials. Now, Beijing is watching the same story play out on the other side of the world.
With less than six weeks until Chinese President Xi Jinping’s planned trip to Washington – his first state visit since 2015 – Beijing finds itself increasingly unsettled by the chaos within the Trump administration.
Sources told the South China Morning Post that Chinese officials were once again confronting a disorganised Trump administration that lacked planning and coordination, with little progress made on hammering out deliverables for the leaders’ summit.
This time, according to the sources, the anxiety runs deeper as the summit will take place on foreign soil.
One person with knowledge of the preparations said that no US official or agency had thus far assumed responsibility for organising the visit, leaving officials on both sides largely engaged in routine preparations without clear leadership.
As was the case with Trump’s trip to Beijing, when the Treasury Department and US Trade Representative played the central roles, the State Department has so far remained largely uninvolved.
The source added that the recent Washington trip by China’s foreign vice-minister Ma Zhaoxu produced a brief improvement in the atmosphere, but that momentum had not been sustained. The official Chinese read-out of the visit said only that Ma held in-depth exchanges with senior US officials.
Two people familiar with the thinking on the Chinese side suggested the issues appeared operational, logistical and optics-related, as neither side had high expectations of achieving anything substantive from the September summit. The only concrete item on the agenda being discussed is a roughly US$30 billion tariff reduction for Chinese goods as a targeted concession.
Chinese officials are particularly sensitive to the dynamics because protocol, venue and public messaging will be largely controlled by the White House, leaving Beijing with less ability to manage the optics or limit surprises.
Sources attributed the slow practical planning to internal deliberations within Trump’s inner circle, where disagreements persist over the tone and framing of the visit. White House advisers like Stephen Miller and Steven Cheung are pushing Trump to project superiority, while others expect the US leader to ease things over with Xi.
All sources spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to comment publicly on the matter.
Trump earlier floated September 24 as the date for Xi’s White House visit, with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio last month indicating that the visit remained on track.
The Chinese leader’s trip comes at a time when the world’s two largest economies are trying to steady ties following the May summit in Beijing, at which Xi and Trump agreed to build what they called a constructive relationship of strategic stability.
That stabilisation has been tested recently, as the two countries trade a series of tit-for-tat measures. Last month, Washington added dozens of Chinese companies to its Uygur Forced Labour Prevention Act entity list, and banned the import and sale of new foreign-made robotic devices and power inverters – sectors in which China is a global leader.
Beijing retaliated by sanctioning seven US entities and tightening export controls on drones and related technology.
US officials have framed the September summit as one of up to four possible meetings between the two leaders this year, and as a chance to stabilise relations and advance cooperation. But the May summit – billed the same way – produced few concrete takeaways.

And it may well be the same this time. According to the sources, a lack of progress has irritated Chinese officials, with one source saying: “There’s not much happening in terms of planning on deliverables.”
Early signs suggest the summit may be thin on concrete results. The US-China Board of Investment – a key outcome of the May talks – was unlikely to be among the deliverables, the SCMP reported this week, noting that neither side had yet initiated the consultation process.
Ali Wyne, a senior research and advocacy adviser on US-China relations at the International Crisis Group, said Chinese officials might be anxious about the apparent lack of planning on the American side because Xi was meeting Trump at a “sensitive juncture” in the US president’s term.
“The United States is bogged down in a war with Iran that is increasingly unpopular with his base, and the Republican Party is bracing for a painful midterm election cycle in just under three months,” Wyne said.
“Trump bristles at the perception that he is losing control of events at home and abroad, and Xi’s advisers may fear that, in an attempt to restore US leverage vis-a-vis China, he will consider making a surprise policy announcement that catches Xi off guard on Trump’s home turf.”

news.title: Trump: I’ll declare Strait of Hormuz a US territory
news.text:
Donald Trump said he would declare the Strait of Hormuz a "territory of the United States" despite having repeatedly failed to reopen it.

The US president on Friday said he would annex the waterway, before suggesting he already controlled it anyway.

Iranian officials accused Mr Trump of indulging in "fanciful delusions".

During a speech in New York on Friday, Mr Trump said: "After we finish defeating Iran, which is being very badly defeated, pretty soon I'll be declaring the Hormuz Strait a territory of the United States. 

"Essentially, that's what it is. We have the blockade. No ships get through unless we want them to."

However, the president also nodded to the economic upheaval unleashed after Iran effectively choked off the strait following the US and Israeli bombing on Feb 28.

Americans would have to pay "a tiny little bit more for your gasoline" as the cost of ensuring a "very evil country" could not develop a nuclear weapon, he said.

Traffic through the strait has slowed to a trickle since the start of the war, and Mr Trump's attempts to reopen it with military forces, economic pressure and diplomacy have failed.

Just nine commercial vessels headed through the waterway on Thursday, according to data firm Kpler, which tracks shipping, compared to pre-war averages of 130 to 140 ships a day.

Securing the strait, which is bordered by Iran and Oman, would almost certainly require boots on the ground, something the president has so far been unwilling to contemplate.

Kazem Gharibabadi, Iran's deputy foreign minister, said Tehran would not be intimidated by the president's rhetoric.

"The Strait of Hormuz cannot be seized by tweet, nor by aircraft carrier, nor by issuing an order, nor by an election speech. Iran neither fears threats nor cowers before displays of power," he said.

Directly addressing the president, he said: "Once and for all, accept the reality: up to this point, you have suffered strategic and heavy defeats; the Strait of Hormuz has been Iranian, is Iranian and will remain Iranian."
